title: Conditionals: Zero, First, Second, Third and Mixed
summary: How to form and use zero, first, second, third and mixed conditionals, the mistakes to avoid, and how if-sentences work in persuasive writing and stories, with practice and answers.

blocks.text: A **conditional** (if-sentence) has two parts: the **if-clause**, which gives the condition, and the **main clause**, which gives the result. *If it rains (condition), the match will be cancelled (result).*

The two clauses can go in either order. **If the if-clause comes first, put a comma after it.** If the main clause comes first, no comma is needed: *If you are hungry, eat something.* / *Eat something if you are hungry.*

blocks.title: Key words
items: **Result / consequence**: what happens because of the condition.
**Real** condition: possible or true. **Unreal** (hypothetical) condition: imagined, unlikely or impossible.

blocks.text: 2. The four main types at a glance

rows: Zero
If + present, present
Facts and things that are always true
If you heat ice, it melts.
First
If + present, will + V1
Real, possible future situations. Warnings, promises
If we plant more trees, the town will be cooler.
Second
If + past simple, would + V1
Unreal or unlikely situations now or in the future. Dreams. Advice
If I were the mayor, I would ban cars from the centre.
Third
If + past perfect, would have + V3
Unreal past: regrets and missed chances
If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
Mixed
If + past perfect, would + V1 (or the reverse)
An unreal past with a result now (or a present fact with a past result)
If I had trained harder, I would be in the team now.

blocks.text: **Zero conditional: always true.** Both verbs are in the present simple. You can usually replace *if* with *when* without changing the meaning: *If / When plants don't get water, they die.* Common in science and information texts.

**First conditional: real future.** The condition is possible. You can use *can, may, might* or an imperative in the main clause: *If you finish early, you can leave.* *If you see Ali, tell him to call me.* *If the wind gets stronger, the ferry might stop.*

**Second conditional: imagined present or future.** The past tense does **not** mean past time here: it shows that the situation is unreal. *If I had a million pounds, I would build a library.* (I don't have it.) Use *could* or *might* for ability or possibility: *If we had more time, we could visit the oasis.*

**Third conditional: imagined past.** Both parts are about a past that did not happen. *If the driver had seen the sign, he would have stopped.* (He didn't see it, so he didn't stop.) Use *could have / might have* for less certain results.

**Mixed conditionals** link different times. Past condition → present result: *If she had taken the job in Dubai, she would be living there now.* Present condition → past result: *If I were more confident, I would have spoken at the meeting.*

rows: unless
if... not
Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus. (= If you don't hurry...)
as long as / provided that
only if
You can borrow my laptop as long as you return it tonight.
in case
because it might happen
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
If only / I wish
a strong wish or regret
If only I had listened! I wish I were taller.
Imagine if...
invites the reader to picture an unreal situation
Imagine if every street had its own garden.
If it will rain, we will stay inside.
If it rains, we will stay inside.
Never put *will* in the if-clause.
If I would have money, I would buy it.
If I had money, I would buy it.
No *would* in the if-clause. Use the past simple.
If I was you, I would apologise.
If I were you, I would apologise.
Use *were* with *I / he / she* in formal second conditionals.
If we would have left earlier, we would have caught it.
If we had left earlier, we would have caught it.
Third conditional: *had* + V3 in the if-clause.
If he had seen it, he would stopped.
If he had seen it, he would have stopped.
The main clause needs *would have* + V3.
Unless you don't study, you will fail.
Unless you study, you will fail.
*Unless* already means *if not*. No second negative.
If you press this button the door opens.
If you press this button, the door opens.
Comma after an if-clause that comes first.

blocks.text: Conditionals are rarely asked about by name, but they are powerful in writing, and you may be asked about their **effect** in a persuasive or fiction text.

items: In persuasive writing, **first conditionals** make consequences sound real and urgent: *If we ignore this problem, our beaches will disappear.*
**Second conditionals** invite the reader to imagine a better (or worse) situation: *If every family recycled, our streets would be cleaner.*
In stories, **third conditionals** show regret: *If only I had listened to her, none of this would have happened.*
**Zero conditionals** state facts in information texts: *If a camel finds water, it can drink more than 100 litres in a few minutes.*

blocks.text: **Exam-style example.** *If we do nothing, the old cinema will be knocked down. If we act now, it will become a home for young artists.*

**Question:** How does the writer use if-sentences to persuade? **Answer:** The writer uses two first conditionals that show opposite results: doing nothing leads to loss, acting leads to something positive. This makes the choice seem simple and urgent and pushes the reader to act.

**In your writing**, use a first conditional to warn or promise in persuasive texts, a second conditional for imagination or advice (*If I were you, I would...*), and a third conditional for a character's regret at the end of a story.

blocks.title: الـ If بسهولة
items: ممنوع will أو would بعد If مباشرة.
حاجة حقيقية ممكن تحصل: If + مضارع ، will.
حاجة خيالية: If + ماضي ، would. وقول If I were مش If I was.
ندم على الماضي: If + had + التصريف التالت ، would have + التصريف التالت.

items.q: Complete with the right conditional: *If I ______ (know) about the party, I would have come.*
Complete: *If you mix blue and yellow, you ______ (get) green.*
items.a: *get* (zero conditional: a fact that is always true).

items.q: Complete: *If it ______ (not rain) tomorrow, we will go to the beach.*
items.a: *doesn't rain* (first conditional: present simple in the if-clause, never *won't rain*).

items.q: Complete: *If I ______ (be) the head teacher, I would make the break longer.*
Correct the mistake: *If we will recycle more, the town will be cleaner.*
items.a: *If we recycle more, the town will be cleaner.* (no *will* in the if-clause).

items.q: Rewrite with *unless*: *If you don't water the plants, they will die.*
items.a: *Unless you water the plants, they will die.*

items.q: Join as a third conditional: *Ahmed didn't set his alarm. He missed the exam.*
items.a: *If Ahmed had set his alarm, he wouldn't have missed the exam.*

items.q: Write a mixed conditional: *Sara didn't learn to swim as a child. She can't join the diving club now.*
items.a: *If Sara had learnt to swim as a child, she could join the diving club now.*

items.q: *If we let the river die, our children will never see the birds that fill it today.* Why is this an effective sentence in a persuasive speech?
items.a: The first conditional presents a real, believable consequence. It links today's choice to the future of *our children*, which makes the reader feel responsible and creates urgency to act now.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: No *will* or *would* straight after *if*. Real = present + will. Unreal = past + would. Regret = had + V3, would have + V3. Comma after a first if-clause.
